subject: biology
title: Principles of homeostasis and thermoregulation
key_idea: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment within narrow limits using receptors, a coordination system and effectors. Negative feedback reverses changes, so levels return to normal. Endotherms control temperature physiologically and behaviourally; ectotherms rely mainly on behaviour.

blocks.text: A multicellular organism has many cells doing different jobs. This section covers why they must communicate and how cells signal.

items: Animals and plants must **respond** to changes in the external environment, such as light, temperature and predators.
They must also respond to changes in the internal environment, such as blood glucose, water potential and temperature.
Different organs must be **coordinated** so that they work together, for example the heart and lungs during exercise.

items.meaning: One cell releasing a signal that changes the activity of another cell.
Signalling between cells next to each other, often through direct contact or short-range chemicals.
Signalling between cells far apart, using a chemical carried in the blood or by nerve impulses.

items: Adjacent cells can signal through direct contact or by releasing a chemical that diffuses a short distance.
Distant cells signal using hormones. These are secreted into the blood, carried round the body and detected by **target cells**.
Target cells have receptors that fit one signal molecule, so only they respond.
Nerve cells signal over long distances by electrical impulses, passing a chemical across each synapse.
Organisms must respond to external and internal changes.
Communication systems coordinate the activity of different organs.
Signals can pass between adjacent cells or between distant cells.

blocks.text: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment steady. This section covers why that matters and how feedback achieves it.

items.meaning: Maintaining the internal environment within restricted limits, in a state of dynamic equilibrium.
A change in the internal or external environment that is detected.
A cell or sensory structure that detects a stimulus and passes information on.
A muscle or gland that carries out a response.
A change is detected and the response reverses it, returning the system to its original level.
A change is detected and the response increases it further, moving the system away from its starting level.

blocks.text: Why a stable internal environment matters

items: **Core temperature** and blood pH affect enzyme activity. Too hot, or too far from the optimum pH, and enzymes denature. Too cold and reactions are slow.
**Blood glucose** must stay steady to supply respiratory substrate to cells.
Blood glucose also affects the water potential of the blood. Too high lowers it, so water leaves cells by osmosis. Too low and cells lack fuel.

diagram.alt: A negative feedback loop: stimulus, receptor, coordination system, effector, response, back to the stimulus.

items: Receptors detect internal and external stimuli and send information to a coordination system.
The coordination systems are the **nervous system** (fast, electrical) and the **endocrine system** (slower, hormonal).
Effectors are muscles and glands. Their response brings the level back towards normal.

rows: Speeds up a process that must finish quickly
Control of body temperature and blood glucose

items: Negative feedback keeps conditions near a set point, with the level swinging slightly either side.
There are **separate mechanisms** for departures in each direction, for example one for a rise and one for a fall. This gives greater control.
Positive feedback is not used for homeostasis because it drives the system away from its normal level.
Homeostasis keeps temperature, pH, glucose and water potential within narrow limits.
Stimulus, receptor, coordinator and effector form the control loop.
Negative feedback reverses a change; positive feedback increases it.

blocks.text: Animals control body temperature in different ways. This section covers endotherms, ectotherms and their responses.

items.meaning: An animal that keeps a stable body temperature using heat from its own metabolism.
An animal that gets most of its body heat from the environment.

items: **Peripheral temperature receptors** in the skin detect changes at the surface.
The **hypothalamus** detects the temperature of the blood and receives information from the skin receptors.
The hypothalamus sends impulses to effectors in the skin and muscles.
Physiological responses are automatic. Behavioural responses are chosen.

diagram.alt: Sort responses into those that happen when the body is too hot and those that happen when it is too cold.
diagram.prompt: Sort each response by when it happens.

items.text: Erector muscles relax so hairs lie flat
Erector muscles contract so hairs stand up

rows: Vasodilation: more blood near the surface, more heat lost
Vasoconstriction: less blood near the surface, less heat lost
Sweat secreted; evaporation cools the skin
Contract so hairs trap an insulating layer of air
Move into shade, remove clothes, reduce activity
Move into the sun, put on clothes, huddle, be more active

items: Ectotherms have few physiological controls, so they rely on **behavioural responses**.
To warm up they bask in the sun, orient their body to the sun or lie on warm rock.
To cool down they move into shade, burrow or enter water.
Their body temperature and activity rise and fall with the environment, but they need far less food than endotherms.
The hypothalamus coordinates temperature control in endotherms, using skin and blood receptors.
Effectors in skin and muscles change heat loss and heat production.
Ectotherms control temperature mainly by behaviour.

checks.q: Distinguish between a receptor and an effector.
checks.a: A receptor detects a stimulus and passes information on. An effector is a muscle or gland that carries out the response.

checks.q: Explain why negative feedback, not positive feedback, is used to control body temperature.
checks.a: Negative feedback reverses a change and returns the temperature to its normal level. Positive feedback would increase the change and move the temperature further from normal, so enzymes would denature.

checks.q: A person in a cold room has narrowed skin arterioles. Explain how this helps them to keep warm.
checks.a: Vasoconstriction means less blood flows to the skin surface. Less heat is lost by radiation, so more heat is kept in the body core.

items: Be ready to read information on a named example and say whether it shows negative or positive feedback.
Negative feedback restores the system to its original level.
Separate mechanisms control departures in each direction. This gives a greater degree of control than one mechanism alone.
Respiration in contracting muscles releases heat, so blood temperature rises during exercise.
The **hypothalamus** detects the raised blood temperature and sends impulses to effectors.
Skin arterioles dilate and sweat glands secrete more sweat, so heat loss increases.
When temperature falls back, heat loss is reduced again. Body temperature fluctuates around a set point: a **dynamic equilibrium**.
Negative feedback keeps the temperature within narrow limits, so enzyme-controlled reactions in muscle cells keep working.
